rationale: I'm replacing the raw Pearson Fisher-z features with a tangent-space embedding of Ledoit-Wolf-shrunk correlation matrices on CC200 (no GSR). The reference point is the Riemannian mean of the training fold only. Abraham 2017 found this was the strongest classic pipeline on ABIDE, because it respects the curved geometry of correlation matrices and centres each subject on the group mean. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm replacing the single CC200 model with an equal-weight ensemble of the same tangent-space and logistic regression pipeline run on four parcellations: CC200, Harvard-Oxford, AAL and Dosenbach160. Each atlas carves the brain up differently, so their connectivity errors should be partly independent, and Abraham 2017 reported that atlas choice changes ABIDE results a lot. Averaging their decision scores should therefore give a more stable signal than any one atlas.

Inter-site differences are the biggest nuisance in ABIDE. Right now every subject is projected around one global geometric mean, so each site's scanner and protocol offset gets mixed into the connectivity features. This change re-centres each site separately (Riemannian Procrustes, as in Zanini 2018 and Ng 2014). Each subject's correlation matrix is whitened by its own site's Riemannian mean, computed label-free from that site's training and test matrices, before mapping to the tangent space at the identity. Site offsets should then disappear while the within-site connectivity differences linked to autism are kept.

The penalty strength C=0.001 was guessed, not tuned. With about 20k standardised tangent features and about 800 subjects, results in this p >> n setting depend heavily on regularisation. This change picks C from a log grid by AUROC in a grouped inner CV that uses only the training fold, with `ctx["groups_train"]` as the groups. The feature pipeline is unchanged.

CC200 may be too coarse to resolve the small, distributed connectivity differences linked to autism. Abraham 2017 found that finer parcellations of around 400 regions usually gave better tangent-space results on ABIDE. This change switches the same Ledoit-Wolf, tangent-space and L2 logistic regression pipeline from CC200 to CC400, the finer parcellation from the same family (~392 ROIs). That tests whether finer spatial resolution adds useful connectivity information, and nothing else changes. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

I'm adding a second view of the same CC200 data. Alongside the current no-GSR pipeline, the same Ledoit-Wolf, tangent-space and logistic regression model is fitted on the global-signal-regressed (`filt_global`) time series. The final score is the average of the two models' decision scores. GSR removes widespread motion and breathing signal but introduces anti-correlations, so the two versions should make partly independent errors on the same strong parcellation. That avoids the problem in round 2, where weaker atlases diluted the CC200 signal. I have not run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.
